subject: cyborgMedic
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: support-hero cyborg medic with a healing staff.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:

Now I'm settling on the details: white armor with teal and gunmetal accents, a glowing gold/cyan caduceus-style healing staff, a cybernetic left eye and arm, swept-back hair blades, and a full humanoid skeleton with spine, clavicle, arm, leg, and finger chains. I'm working out the rest pose, deciding on a loose A-pose with the staff held in the right hand and fingers separated.

I'm calculating the arm reach to position the staff: planting it vertically beside the right hand, checking shoulder-to-hand distances against arm segment lengths to make sure the hand can realistically grip the shaft, and simplifying the finger curl around the staff radius to keep the rig manageable.

I'll make the left hand open with extended fingers for a readable rest pose, while the right hand loosely curls around the staff using simple 3-point finger chains. Now I'm starting to lay out the joint builder with hip position and body proportions like head height relative to total height.

Working out leg geometry now—hip, knee, and ankle positions with thigh and shin lengths slightly exceeding the hip-to-ankle distance so the knee bends naturally rather than locking straight.

Then I need to add the foot joint, attaching the toe to the ankle chain's tip, and settle on a side convention where +X represents the model's left side.

I'll keep most placements in model-space coordinates using constants for the head center, letting parts attach to the nearest joint automatically while explicitly specifying the bone for head parts. For the torso, I'm planning to use a loft over the spine chain with stations defining width and height at each joint position.

I'm building out the skeleton: a spine chain running from the hips joint upward through several stations, a short neck chain, and a head joint positioned slightly forward and up, where I need to think through the head's orientation for correct part attachment.

Placing the jaw hinge at the back-bottom of the head aimed forward, then setting up head dimensions with a constant head center point and a skull sphere slightly flattened and scaled for a stylized Overwatch-like proportion.

Now I'm shaping the face features: a lower jaw as a rigid chin wedge, upper face with cheekbones built from scaled spheres on either side, a small nose cone, and a defined brow, all positioned relative to the skull center for that smooth heroic look.

For eyes I'm thinking decal textures placed onto the skull surface—a human-looking right eye and a glowing cyan cybernetic left eye with a reticle effect. I'm also settling on a character concept: a warm brown-skinned figure with swept-back silver-white hair and a cybernetic left eye, giving her a stern but approachable medic-hero vibe, something like "Dr. Halcyon Vey."

For the mouth, I'm sketching a simple jaw piece and a thin dark line decal to suggest lips, deciding decals work best applied directly onto the curved skull surface near the face rather than as flat planes.

I'm working out the exact coordinates for the eye decals so they sit properly on the curved skull surface above the cheek spheres, calculating the z-depth using the sphere's curvature formula and making sure the brow ridge and cheeks are positioned below without overlapping the eyes.

Now I'm planning out the full module structure: palettes, paint definitions, texture overlays for eyes (human and cyber variants), plus emblem elements like a medical cross and caduceus, and tech panel-line details -- aiming for a thorough but correct implementation across several hundred lines.

I'm sketching the remaining textures and gear pieces: hex-pattern armor trim, a glowing orb texture for a staff, feather cards for staff wings, a tabard with a cross emblem, a satchel and medkit, pauldrons, a glowing "healing core" on the chest, and a floating backpack emitter with fins. Then I'm breaking down the body construction starting with the pelvis and torso loft, defining stations from hips to chest for the silhouette.

Now I'm detailing the remaining anatomy and gear: a separate armor chest plate over a dark undersuit, a high collar ring with teal trim, hair and head details, pauldrons as half-dome shapes with cross decals, and arms split between an armored white right gauntlet and an exposed cybernetic left arm with glowing cyan segments and pistons. I'm also planning the legs with dark thigh suits, white greaves, boots, and a belt with pouches and glowing green medical canisters, before moving on to the back attachments.

I'm designing the backpack with glowing biotic emitter cylinders and an antenna, a caduceus-style staff with intertwined spiral sweeps around a glowing orb and extruded wings, plus a cape/tabard made of two cloth panels extruded from the belt, all set in a relaxed A-pose with arms angled outward. Now I'm working through the chain creation API, figuring out how a polyline of points maps to named joints like shoulder, elbow, and wrist for the arm rig.

I'm sorting out the limb function's parameters — root and target points, segment lengths, and bend directions — and how bends can be given as a single direction vector or a list per joint, which I'll use to curve the elbow backward and outward for the staff-holding arm. I'm also placing the clavicle joint relative to the spine for proper shoulder positioning.

Now I'm computing the shoulder-to-hand geometry for an A-pose arm, checking that the upper arm plus forearm length roughly matches the distance to the target hand position so the elbow bend stays natural, adjusting the hand target slightly to keep the reach just under full length.

For the right arm holding the staff, I'm positioning the wrist target and offsetting the hand center along the forearm direction so the grip sits correctly around the staff shaft, placing the shaft axis near the hand so the fist appears to wrap around it.

I'm figuring out the fist orientation as a small capsule/box at the wrist joint, with fingers curling around the front of the shaft and the palm pressed against the inner side facing the body.

Each finger will be a curved arc chain wrapping around the shaft, built as three joints following a path, and I'll repeat this for four fingers plus a thumb on the right hand, naming each chain accordingly.

Mapping out the finger arc geometry around the shaft center with angles sweeping from the palm side to the far side, then positioning the palm box relative to the shaft and finger roots.

Simplifying the grip itself feels wiser here - I'm reconsidering whether to just use a basic fist shape (box plus sphere) for the hand holding the staff, rather than wrestling with precise finger joint placement for such a small visual detail.

Computing shoulder-to-wrist distance gives a bent elbow, which works fine for the staff-holding arm. Now I'm setting up the left hand with an open palm, four separated finger chains plus a thumb, positioned to hang down with the palm facing inward toward the thigh.

Still wiring up finger chains and parenting them to the wrist joint. I'm tallying the total joint count across legs, spine, neck, head, arms, and fingers to make sure the skeleton stays manageable, landing somewhere around 38 just for the hands.

For the staff, I'll rigidly attach it to the right wrist bone so arm motion carries it naturally, checking that the ferrule still rests near floor level. Now I'm turning to the spine, planning to build it as a loft through station centers with interpolated width and height along an elliptical cross-section.

For the vertical path, width maps to the sideways (binormal) radius and depth to the front-back (normal) radius, matching the default roll orientation. The loft should start just below where the spine chain begins, so it rides naturally with the first bone.

For the torso material, I'm planning a navy undersuit with teal piping, using a shading helper that mixes darker and lighter tones based on the up-facing normal plus subtle noise, pulling in mix/noise/paint utilities from the SDK's exports.

For the cyber arm, I'll pull in the glow kit and clockwork's metal kit, going with a steel finish and skipping gear texture details to keep things simpler. The armor itself gets a white base with a cool blue shade on the underside and some edge wear for visual interest.

Now I'm working through imports from the agentic-3js-builder module, pulling in the core functions I need like frame, line, paint, mix, noise, and gradient, while avoiding most type imports to keep things clean.

Instead I'm settling on separating the head into three parts stacked vertically: a smaller cranium sphere positioned higher up, a mid-face block for the cheeks and nose area down to the mouth line, and the lower jaw/chin section below that, all sized so the heights add up correctly. I'm starting to lay out the actual coordinates and radii for the cranium sphere and the upper face block.

Checking lower down, the midface does protrude slightly below cheekbone height, but that's expected for the cheek shape. The eye decal sits mostly on the cranium surface with only a sliver of overlap near the bottom edge, which should be negligible.

Now I'm planning the small facial features: a compact four-sided cone for the nose tip pointing forward and slightly up, skipping nostril detail; small flattened spheres for the ears, with the left ear getting a cyborg headset piece (white earcup with teal glow and a thin antenna) while the right stays human; and a white plated slab on the left cheek for the cybernetic plate.

For the cheek plate, rather than a floating flat slab that would awkwardly intersect the curved face geometry, I'm switching to using a decal projected in the +X direction to cover the left temple and cheek region, so the panel lines and teal highlight wrap naturally onto the curved surface.

Working out the viewing geometry, since the viewer looks in the -X direction with +Y up, the drawing's right side corresponds to world -Z (back of head) and the drawing's left corresponds to +Z (front of face) — so I need to position the plate design with its front edge toward the left of the decal.

Now moving on to the eyebrows (simple sweeping shapes) and then the hair: I'm planning a swept-back silver-white style built from a solid base cap, a sphere scaled slightly larger than the cranium to sit over it.

So I'm considering tilting the whole hair cap backward around the x-axis so the hairline sits higher at the forehead and drops lower toward the nape, since a straight horizontal rim leaves the sides poking through the cranium at the front but gapping at the sides.

Checking the forehead region, the hair surface comes out closer to center than the cranium surface at that height, meaning the hair would clip inside the skull rather than cover it — so I need to increase the hair's z-scale to keep it properly outside the cranium at the front.

Adding pompadour swoosh blades using tapered tube sweeps along bezier curves from forehead to back, at varying x offsets for volume...
